finding.claim: PUT /me mass-assigns the entire request body onto the persisted user object, so any authenticated user can overwrite arbitrary user fields (e.g. role, isAdmin, tenantId, id, password hash) if those fields exist in the user schema. Probable privilege escalation / account takeover; severity depends on the schema, which is not in the repo.
finding.source: users.js:4 PUT /me, req.body (all JSON keys, attacker-controlled)
finding.sink: users.js:5 Object.assign(req.user, req.body), persisted by users.js:6 req.store.save(req.user)

trace.note: Object.assign copies every own key of req.body onto req.user with no allowlist
req.store.save persists the mutated user object
Response echoes the modified user record

finding.guards_checked: No field allowlist, schema validation, or key filtering in users.js. The /me/profile handler (users.js:10-13) uses an allowlist, but /me does not. Authentication middleware that populates req.user and protects the route is outside the repo and was not verified.

verdict.guard_found: None in users.js. Lines 4-7 match the candidate: users.js:5 Object.assign(req.user, req.body) has no key filtering, users.js:6 saves req.user, and users.js:7 echoes it. The /me/profile handler at users.js:10-12 uses an allowlist, but that does not guard /me. The auth middleware that populates req.user is not in the repo, and no schema or store code is present.
verdict.reason: The mass-assignment at users.js:5 is real and unguarded in this repo, and the attacker is presumably an authenticated user editing their own record, but whether it is a privilege escalation depends on whether role, isAdmin, tenantId, or similar fields exist in the store schema (outside the repo) and on the auth middleware that sets req.user (also outside the repo), so impact cannot be decided from the available code.

finding.claim: PUT /me/profile is a partial update that silently clears fields: destructured keys absent from the body become undefined, and Object.assign copies undefined values, so sending only bio erases displayName. Stored displayName and bio are also not type- or length-checked.
finding.sink: users.js:12 Object.assign(req.user, { displayName, bio }), persisted by users.js:13 req.store.save(req.user)

trace.note: Destructures displayName and bio from req.body; missing keys become undefined
Object.assign copies undefined values, overwriting existing stored fields

finding.guards_checked: Field allowlisting is enforced (only displayName and bio are copied). No type, length, or undefined-value checks. Logic flaw with data loss and unbounded input, low severity; no direct privilege impact from this file.

verdict.guard_found: Field allowlisting at users.js:12 (only displayName and bio are copied). It does not stop undefined values from overwriting stored fields, and there are no type or length checks on those values anywhere in users.js.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: users.js:11 destructures the keys, users.js:12 Object.assign copies undefined values over existing fields, and users.js:13 persists the result, so a partial PUT to /me/profile clears displayName. The effect is limited to the caller's own record and is a low-severity logic flaw, not a privilege issue. The auth middleware that sets req.user is not in the provided code, so I could not confirm that req.user is always the caller's own record.
